title: Building a solo tabletop RPG setup where Claude runs the game inside Foundry VTT: what the AI built for itself, and what still breaks (free downloads)
author: DungeonTurn
selftext:
Disclosure: I run *Dungeon Turn*, a new YouTube channel about solo tabletop RPGs with an AI as the GM. The video and the kit below are mine. The kit is free under the MIT license, and nothing is for sale or behind a paywall.

So, I know the jam here is mostly video games, but this is a solution for playing TTRPGs with AI - and yes, this version works. *This is not another "I tried AI as the DM so you don't have to" complaint.*  

Complaints from other people about using AI as a DM: A chat-only AI GM loses track of the numbers, can't keep secrets, improvises stories that fall apart, and is hopelessly sycophantic. **What worked for me** was splitting the job into a modularized architecture. Foundry VTT (v14, with the Pathfinder 2e system) owns every number: rolls, HP, conditions, loot. Plain notes in Obsidian own the memory: rulings, prep, where we stopped, what the party knows. A human-written adventure owns the story. Claude, through its desktop app, sits in between as the GM, joined to Foundry as the Gamemaster in a Chrome tab. 

**This solution improved secret-keeping, eliminated AI sycophancy, and let me run crunchy PF2e combat error-free.**

***Development Notes:***

My big role in all of this was asking the AI if it could drive FoundryVTT programmatically, through an API. Once it said the equivalent of "yeah, duh," I gave it an adventure to run and let it actually do prep, like a human DM would. Most of the tooling, the AI built for itself as we played. It wrote a small Foundry module it drives for creature turns, reaction windows, roll requests and line of sight. Regions over doors, traps and clues pause the game when a token steps in, and the AI takes the scene; region behaviors are what made exploration work at all. When something goes wrong mid-session I say so out of game, it goes on a fix list, and it gets fixed before the next session.

**What still doesn't work:** 

1) the AI talks to itself in the chat, which can leak spoilers. It's rare but it happens. Spoken narration with a local Kokoro voice helps, because the AI stages deliberate dialogue much better than it controls its self-talk. I've almost got this fixed by having the AI send DELIBERATE messages to the VTT chat, so I don't look at the AI's chat window except to press the dictation button. 

2) I still haven't gotten an AI-controlled DMPC to work correctly. It does fine running the combat but if you allow it to roleplay, the DMPC starts spilling secrets, which is odd since I seem to have solved secret keeping otherwise.

**The biggest lesson so far:** an AI improvising a whole sandbox TTRPG is awful. Give it a human-written backbone and it gets good.

The video walks through every piece of the setup, with region triggers in play (32 minutes, with chapters): [https://youtu.be/\_agaDCVuzzI](https://youtu.be/_agaDCVuzzI)

The instructions, session skills and Foundry module are in a free kit. Point your AI at AI-README.md in the download and it walks you through setup. Tested only with Claude Code, Foundry VTT v14 and PF2e. A free example adventure is a separate download on the same page: https://dungeonturn.itch.io/solo-ai-gm-starter-kit

Has anyone gotten an AI-played companion to roleplay without spilling what it knows? Separate context, a separate agent, something else?

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body: the split is right imo. similar setup here, the engine owns HP and rolls and the model only narrates. what still slips through is prose drifting from state, the other night it called an enemy unconscious while the engine had him at 9 of 20. the engine number wins on screen, the text just stays wrong

replies.author: DungeonTurn
replies.body: Interesting - I haven’t had it misread rolls in the VTT yet. If the action is fast it might miss a re-roll (like with a hero point) though. What are you playing and what model do you use for the narration?
